Since I happen to have time today, I’ll explain some key points about project management. As the company’s business grows, some small-scale projects next year may no longer be managed by me directly. You already have some experience, and since all of you hold the title of Project Manager, you can independently oversee certain small projects. Considering you might lack project management experience, this training will briefly cover relevant topics. Of course, a single session can’t cover everything—feel free to consult me, Double, or other colleagues if specific issues arise later.

First, let’s outline the basic workflow of a design project. As this was decided spontaneously, I haven’t prepared a PPT today. The project workflow typically starts from securing the project until its final completion, and even simple projects involve multiple stages.

Opportunity acquisition falls under marketing, but when a client requests a quote, it enters the business development phase—the stage of preparing a bid proposal. This training will focus on the workflow starting from opportunity acquisition.

Take government or large-scale projects we’ve won in the past as examples. These are usually announced via relevant websites. We regularly check these, filter for projects that interest us and align with our capabilities, download the tender documents for evaluation (including technical feasibility, resource availability, and scheduling), and finally decide whether to bid.

However, most of our projects are small-scale, such as private-sector projects in residential, commercial, or industrial categories. Currently, these projects often come from clients reaching out proactively via phone or email to gauge our interest. Today’s training will focus on the management process for such projects.

For this type of project, I typically receive inquiries via phone or email, where the client outlines the project requirements through calls, emails, or WeChat. What they primarily seek are electrical design services. They provide details such as project type, location, and basic specifications, and share relevant drawings via email—such as architectural plans, mechanical diagrams, or site photos.

In the early stages, I would conduct on-site visits before providing quotes. However, I later realized this approach was inefficient—if only 50 out of 100 projects materialized, it meant 50 site visits were wasted. With accumulated experience, I can now estimate the scope and quote range (e.g., $2,000–$3,000 for small projects) based on project descriptions alone. As a result, we now provide direct quotes for small to medium-sized projects.

Handling 300 proposals annually would require significant time if the volume increased to 800 the next year. Assuming each site visit takes 3 hours, this alone would consume a full-time employee’s workload. Clearly, this is not cost-effective. We’ve shifted to quoting based on client-provided materials, as price variations for such small projects are limited.

For large-scale projects (e.g., spanning tens of thousands of square feet), on-site visits remain necessary. However, new residential projects can usually be quoted based solely on architectural drawings and client requirements. If a site visit is conducted, we recommend capturing ample photos and videos—this helps form a comprehensive understanding and serves as reference material for other team members. For instance, if the project lead is unavailable, these visual records provide clearer project insights.

Currently, larger proposals are handled by dedicated teams, such as the one led by Vera.

Government projects typically require proposals exceeding ten pages, usually ranging between ten to twenty pages. Our company has a dedicated team responsible for such proposals. You only need to prepare three to five pages of content and modify certain sections based on the existing template. I will provide further details later.

The proposal contains several key sections requiring special attention, starting with the Scope of Work. When communicating with clients, it is essential to clarify whether the responsibility lies in electrical design, mechanical design, or other areas. If it involves electrical design, confirm the specifics: whether it covers power systems, lighting, fire alarm systems entirely, or only a portion. For example, some projects may require only the Ashley section, the completion of Schedule B, or a focus solely on the fire alarm system. These boundaries must be clearly defined.

Additionally, the project may involve different phases. For example, we might only handle the BCHydro coordination portion. The Scope of Work directly determines the project’s boundaries and the basis for pricing. Another critical aspect is the client’s specific requirements. Taking a TI project as an example, the client might request tasks like installing a dishwasher, replacing a water heater, updating light fixtures or retaining existing ones, or upgrading the electrical panel. Such details must be clearly outlined in the Scope of Work.

A detailed Scope of Work offers two main advantages: First, it helps prevent disputes later on. Second, it enables other colleagues (e.g., Blake or Double) to quickly grasp the project’s scope when taking over. Our company provides a dedicated proposal template for reference. While the current template is relatively simple, it meets basic needs adequately.

The proposal is typically stored in the proposal folder and categorized by year. Its naming convention is generally consistent with that of the project.

This section displays the project status, including submitted, unsubmitted, rejected, or successful. We can freely open a recent record to view, as there is nothing particularly special about these contents.

This is extremely important—to provide a concise overview of the project. The content should include details such as the project type, location, purpose (e.g., residential or tenant improvement), total area, number of floors, parking configuration (if applicable), unit count (e.g., for apartment projects), and other relevant information. Describe these details as thoroughly as possible to facilitate subsequent database entry and team comprehension.

Additionally, list any relevant assumptions and existing conditions, for example:
- Architectural CAD drawings are provided by the client
- Mechanical CAD drawings are provided by the client
- Structural CAD drawings are provided by the client
- Electrical load information is provided by the client

Work typically begins after receiving a 30% or 50% advance payment. The project duration will be determined based on the receipt of complete documentation and the project schedule, which may span two weeks or another reasonable timeframe.

Clearly define the scope of engineering services, specifying the work to be completed.

During the design process, the Scope of Work serves as the specification document provided to contractors. As part of the consulting design services, the services being offered to the client must be clearly outlined.

For instance, the document should specify attending at least one on-site meeting to confirm site conditions, scope of work, or any special requirements from the client.

Secondly, review the design requirements with clients and other professional teams. Additionally, electrical load calculations must be completed.

The fourth point involves designing lighting, power supply, communication, alarm, access control systems, and the parts that provide power to mechanical equipment. These elements can be adjusted according to the specific requirements of the project.

This means the total working hours are capped at 40 hours, so the hours submitted to BC Hydro will also be 40. This cost is already included in the design fee. If the hours exceed 40, additional fees may be claimed.

Please note that this is a contract with legal binding force. Once signed by both parties, it must be executed accordingly. If actual working hours exceed the agreed amount, a change order must be submitted to the other party. If challenged, records can be provided to prove the excess hours.

Next is the allocation of hours for coordination and communication, as well as the design of the power distribution system, electrical room layout, outdoor landscape or building perimeter, public area lighting layout, circuit design, and other related tasks.

Under normal circumstances, in development projects (such as a building), we clearly define the scope of responsibilities. The areas within the building’s property line are our responsibility, while street lighting design falls outside the property line and is therefore typically excluded.

If the client requires street lighting services, we provide a separate quotation. Since street lighting involves considerable coordination and collaboration, we generally do not include it in our standard pricing.

As for external lighting or landscape lighting, these fall within the design scope of the property line.

Suite layouts, which refer to the enlarged drawings of each unit in residential projects. It should be noted here as production of electrical building permit drawings.

For such small to medium-sized projects, we typically only complete the design work up to the building permit stage. The subsequent Issued for Construction (IFC) drawings are often not produced separately; the client will directly use the building permit drawing package for tendering and construction. Of course, if design changes arise during construction, we will make the necessary modifications accordingly.

It should be noted that the above process applies only to small/medium-sized or private projects.

The above process applies only to small/medium-sized or private projects.  

The workflow for government projects is entirely different, with significantly increased complexity. We explicitly inform clients that the base submission includes four sets of drawings. Additional printed drawings are charged at a rate of five Canadian dollars per sheet. Furthermore, a professional liability insurance certificate must be provided.  

The reason we can undertake these projects and charge fees is that we have already invested significant costs. Taking professional liability insurance as an example, other companies might need to pay $10,000, whereas our annual cost is approximately $7,000. Obtaining such insurance certificates requires financial investment, so it is reasonable for us to charge clients accordingly. Additionally, maintaining company certifications also demands ongoing annual financial commitments.

Our service scope includes:  
1. Electrical Building Schedule preparation  
2. Electrical Shop Drawing Review  
3. Electrical Field Review  

For standalone Schedule B preparation services, we charge accordingly because it involves technical liability. Shop drawing reviews are particularly critical, as they confirm the suitability of drawings before equipment orders are placed. Such reviews should typically be included in the service scope unless it’s a minor renovation project (e.g., replacing a panelboard or small circuit breaker).

Engineers bear significant responsibility in this process. Once a project is signed, they are accountable for all technical electrical aspects of the building—not just completing the design. While not reviewing drawings may not constitute direct liability, indirect responsibility may still apply. This reflects the dual nature of an engineer’s role in projects: substantial authority comes with equally substantial responsibility.

Of course, you also have the right to clearly refuse to sign and request a replacement, and the other party must comply. Therefore, this issue requires serious attention.

You also have the right to clearly refuse to sign and request a replacement, and the other party must comply. Therefore, this issue requires serious attention.

Our fees are not solely based on the number of drawings—for example, charging two thousand yuan for what may seem like a few simple drawings, with each sheet costing one thousand yuan. Behind this lies numerous responsibilities and risks, commonly referred to as “liability.” As such, we typically conduct an Electrical Field Review, which also falls within the engineer’s scope of duties and requires you to assume the corresponding responsibility.

The above-listed items constitute our scope of services provided to clients. Below are specifically listed services not included in this project, meaning these tasks fall outside our responsibilities. If clients require such services, they can be negotiated separately.

For example, lighting fixture selection, road lighting design, smart home system design, and bid document review during the tendering process are typically included in government projects but are generally not provided for residential projects. Additionally, tasks such as applying for electrical construction permits, estimating construction costs, and preparing as-built drawings are also outside our service scope.

Our primary responsibilities include design review, on-site inspections, and commissioning acceptance, but we do not cover specific installation matters such as fire alarm system verification.

It is necessary to clarify another cost item, and specifically note: Any electrical engineering work not included in the current scope does not fall under our responsibility. This means that, in the final interpretation, all unmentioned items are outside our scope of responsibility.

Upon completion of the above scope of work, the design fee will be determined. This fee includes four design meetings and six site visits or reviews. Any additional meetings or site visits will be charged at CAD 350 each (excluding GST).

If modifications are required, billing can be hourly or re-quoted, and work will proceed after confirmation. Below are the hourly rate references for each position, though we typically adopt a fixed-fee model rather than hourly billing.

Next, it is crucial to clarify how fees will be collected, which is particularly important for accountants and project managers. The key lies in understanding which stage the project has reached and promptly notifying the finance department to issue invoices.

For example, the first payment is a 30% deposit before design work begins, which should be paid immediately after the invoice is issued. The second stage occurs when submitting the building permit application—once submitted, an invoice for 40% or the corresponding proportion should be issued without delay.

The signing letter above indicates that the project can commence once both parties reach an agreement. While this contract is relatively concise, it is sufficient for small and medium-sized projects. In contrast, formal contracts signed with government entities or other large organizations may span dozens of pages.

After completing the above content, the next step is to discuss the quotation issue.

Typically, for TI projects, the electrical engineering cost in the Vancouver area is approximately CAD 0.6 to 0.8 per square foot. Of course, the larger the project scale, the lower the unit price may be.

Typically, for TI projects, the electrical engineering cost in the Vancouver area is approximately CAD 0.6 to 0.8 per square foot. Of course, the larger the project scale, the lower the unit price may be.

However, for very small projects, such as a small restaurant with only 500 square feet, we cannot charge solely based on area. Therefore, we have a minimum fee standard, where P4P3 category projects have a minimum charge of CAD 2000. Even if the project is smaller, we will still charge the standard fee of CAD 2000.

This is a special fee standard determined through negotiation. Thus, even for projects ranging from 500 to 600 square feet, the minimum charge remains CAD 2000.

The pricing is not calculated based on the number of times. Generally speaking, our minimum charge is 2000 CNY. Specifically, for projects under 2000 square feet, the minimum charge is 2000 CNY. However, in reality, for most projects around 1000+ square feet, our fee is typically 2500 CNY.

Current market quotes typically range around 2,000 yuan, depending on project requirements. For instance, we recently undertook a project in Langley quoted at 2,600 yuan, but the client reported another company’s offer of just 1,700 yuan. After negotiations, we adjusted to 2,300 yuan, but the client ultimately chose another provider.

Looking back to 2017 or 2018, a 1,500-square-foot office renovation project in Surrey was referred by an architect. We initially quoted 2,000 yuan but agreed to reduce the price due to limited project experience. After multiple negotiations, we lowered it to 1,600 yuan, but the client ultimately awarded the project to a competitor at 800 yuan.

Regarding price undercutting, a rational approach is essential. While it may help sustain short-term operations, it harms the market in the long run. For instance, in the Cosada project, we initially quoted 2,800 yuan but adjusted to 2,500 yuan under competitor pressure. However, in a subsequent project, the client questioned the price difference, which directly undermined market trust. Therefore, we maintain fair pricing to prevent恶性竞争 (cutthroat competition).

Our company’s current stage of development no longer permits excessive compromise. Low-price projects may keep the team busy but cannot cover operational costs. For instance, an 800-yuan project requires multiple site visits, blueprint printing, etc., with actual costs far exceeding revenue. Thus, we firmly reject unreasonable low bids to uphold industry standards and sustainable growth.

Additionally, this is TI’s work. If it only involves individual services such as scanulb 500 or transformal ledger 500, or just flow alarm, the pricing method needs to be adjusted. For example, if a project includes three services—flow alarm, lighting, and power—with a total price of 2,400 yuan, the unit service price would be approximately 800 yuan. However, if only the flow alarm service is provided, the price should be around 1,200 yuan, reflecting a 50% increase due to additional work such as standalone project management and drawing output.

For residential projects, the pricing is related to the project scale. The larger the project, the lower the unit area cost. For instance, in an earlier unfinished project spanning over 100,000 square feet, the total price was just over 20,000 yuan, with a unit area cost of about 0.2 to 0.25 yuan. Currently, due to intense market competition, the unit area cost for apartment projects typically ranges between 0.3 and 0.4 yuan, and the larger the project, the lower the unit area cost.

The typical price per square foot ranges from 30 to 40 cents, for example, in a 100,000-square-foot project. It’s very difficult to reach a rate of 50 cents per square foot—30 to 40 cents is already considered quite good. Later-phase townhouse developments also follow this basic standard.

For townhouse projects with around 20 units, the standard fee generally ranges from 600 to 800 yuan. For smaller projects, such as townhouses with only six units, the fee is set at 1,000 yuan. These small-scale projects are often not cost-effective—either the workload is insufficient or they consume too much time and effort.

Overall, it is challenging to increase fees for residential projects. Regarding final pricing, I will review and make the decision before submission.

In light of certain special circumstances, such as long-term cooperative clients or the importance of the project, we can adjust the price at our discretion.

Additionally, some clients prefer to negotiate. After receiving a quote, they may request price matching with offers from other companies. Even if you agree, they will continue to push for further discounts, creating an endless cycle.

Additionally, some clients prefer to negotiate. After receiving a quote, they may request price matching with offers from other companies. Even if you agree, they will continue to push for further discounts, creating an endless cycle.

For such projects, we set a bottom line. Once this line is reached, we terminate the cooperation. These clients are often not high-quality customers.

Regarding price negotiations, we typically allow a 5% to 10% flexibility range. If the adjustment is too large—for example, dropping from 30,000 yuan to 15,000 yuan—it may instead suggest that the initial quote was inflated. A reasonable flexibility range should be between 5% and 20%, which demonstrates willingness to cooperate while maintaining the professionalism of the pricing.

Excessive discounts not only fail to convey benefits but also raise doubts about the true value of the quote. These are some considerations in pricing strategy.

After creating folders in both Send and Inbox, the basic setup is complete, and work can begin. As a Project Manager (PM), several key issues need to be clarified. For example, once the Work Group (WG) is established, an 8G file will be generated. In the project database, typical time allocations may include 20 hours for designers, 3 hours for review, 2 hours for engineers, and 3 hours for the project manager, among others. At this stage, the PM must ensure the project is completed within budget—Cost Management—while also controlling the project timeline—Schedule Management.

The PM must confirm the primary design provider (e.g., the architect or client) with the client or the Prime Consultant (typically from the mechanical discipline). At project initiation, a Kick-off Meeting is held to officially launch the project, introduce team members, and discuss the budget and division of responsibilities. The meeting will determine key milestones, such as the deadline for the first IFR submission.

When attending meetings, focus on the key discussion points. For instance, when discussing schedules—such as inquiring about the submission timelines for architectural and mechanical drawings—the Electrical (Electro) discipline typically submits last. Proper time planning is crucial here; blindly following other disciplines’ schedules is not advisable. For smaller projects, such as Tenant Improvement (TI) projects, an additional week is usually required for processing. This extra week is used to receive architectural drawings, client equipment lists, mechanical drawings, and other necessary documents.

For medium-sized projects, completion typically requires one week. International teams may need one to two weeks, whereas we usually finish within a week. TI projects and other small-scale projects can be completed within three days. For large projects, such as apartment buildings, at least one to two weeks are necessary. Although clients may disagree with a two-week timeline, it is essential to insist on a minimum of one week to demonstrate professionalism and reliability. Showing uncertainty or needing to consult superiors can undermine client trust.

As a professional collaborator, extensive experience is required. Clients must be clearly informed that residential projects require architectural drawings, along with details such as specific application scenarios, appliance types, and heating methods. Without these critical documents, the project cannot proceed.

During the initial phase of a new project, it is crucial to emphasize early involvement of the electrical team in coordinating with BC Hydro. Delays in coordination will impact the overall timeline. When working with BC Hydro, load information must be provided, including configurations for electrical rooms, transformers, and other equipment. Additionally, clients must prepare various forms and complete account application procedures. These are key scheduling and coordination points that project managers must master.

For TI projects, basic architectural drawings must be obtained. However, note that these drawings may contain errors and often undergo changes during construction. Therefore, we typically conduct on-site surveys and document findings with photos. Scheduling an appointment with the client is necessary before the survey to obtain the latest drawings. For food service projects, equipment lists must also be requested.

During the design phase, coordination with mechanical and architectural teams is required to align drawings and confirm the BP (Building Plan) format—whether digital or hardcopy.

During the specific implementation process, we need to focus on three key aspects: firstly, controlling the BP process, secondly, meeting digitalization requirements, and simultaneously ensuring quality compliance.

Quality control involves multiple dimensions:
1. The design scheme must not contain any fundamental major issues;
2. The quality of drawings needs improvement, including cleanliness of the layout and clarity of expression;
3. Strictly enforce the existing checklist.

It is recommended that each engineer prints the checklist and creates a dedicated folder to systematically perform checks, whether during design reviews or BP submissions.

OK, thank you, bye.

It is recommended that each engineer prints the checklist and creates a dedicated folder to systematically perform checks, whether during design reviews or BP submissions.

A fee of 200 yuan is required to obtain the license, which is unavoidable. As the project manager, you must carefully review and take responsibility for the documentation of these small-scale projects. This includes: verifying whether there are errors or omissions in the printed drawings and confirming if the seals are correctly affixed. For example, drawings for British Columbia will be invalid if mistakenly stamped with Ontario’s seal.

In British Columbia, the two most common issues are as follows:  
1. Incorrect addresses, usually caused by clients or architects, or due to our own oversight. Therefore, thorough verification is essential before final submission.  
2. Misuse of Schedule B forms. For instance, the City One Core project has its dedicated form—using the provincial form by mistake will result in rejection. Additionally, when the building code was updated from the 2012 version to the 2018 version at the end of December 2019, continued use of the old forms would also lead to rejection. Project managers must master these key points.

Document management is equally important. After formal submissions at each project stage (e.g., IFR, ILB), corresponding records such as “IFR,” “REIFR1,” “REIFR2,” etc., should be created in the project folder, with dates marked for traceability. During the design phase, project updates must also be noted. For example, upon receiving an email requesting BP resubmission, prompt action is required, and the project database should indicate BP approved, marking the project’s transition to the construction phase.

In other words, after their construction team receives this set of construction drawings, will they notify us?

If no notification is received, please follow up promptly by phone or email. If time is limited, it can be temporarily left unaddressed. If the application is not approved, the other party will proactively reach out. As a project manager, tracking progress falls within your responsibilities, so it’s advisable to follow up appropriately.

But at this point in time, when the DM signs off?

No, after signing the contract, modifications may be required once the Building Permit (BP) is submitted. If the modifications are requested by the city government, we usually do not charge a fee; however, if they are requested by the client (Party A) or arise due to changes during the construction process, we will charge accordingly.

After obtaining the building permit, the project moves into the construction phase. For typical small-scale projects, especially Tenant Improvement (TI) projects, we usually conduct a rough-in inspection. As you know, we visit the site and prepare a report. But for very small projects, such as pizza shops, we might skip the rough-in inspection and proceed directly to the final inspection.

For large-scale projects, we still conduct a rough-in inspection, while small-scale projects may go straight to the final inspection. During the final inspection, we take photos and assess the construction quality. Typically, before the final inspection, we require two documents: one is the fire alarm verification report, to ensure there are no defects or errors in the system.

Secondly, regarding the electrical inspector’s report, this part is the contractor’s responsibility to arrange personnel for inspection. The inspector will submit the report to the electrical contractor, who in turn must provide us with the approved inspection report. These two documents are mandatory for us.

Normally, we expect both reports to be submitted in full. However, in the Greater Vancouver area, Surrey has a unique requirement where Schedule C must be submitted first to obtain the electrical inspection report. Additionally, the electrical inspection process in Greater Vancouver is quite disorganized—for example, City1Core has its own inspectors, while Richmond does not.

Whether all reports are collected or not, on-site inspections in Surrey or other cities require taking photos. These photos serve not only as records but also as potential marketing materials in the future. Note that the photos in inspection reports are usually of poor quality and unsuitable for direct promotional use. However, retaining them is necessary—for instance, they can serve as proof of field inspections during EGBC audits. Moreover, the inspection reports themselves must also include photos.
